The UK debut of the stage show has been a long time coming, but is absolutely worth the wait.
DREAMGIRLS, charting the rise to success of a 1960's Supremes-style girl group 'The Dreams', crackles along at a lively pace with plenty of soul, sass and colour.

Dreamgirls is not my kind of musical, since my basic taste runs to sophisticated and small scale. This is huge, incredibly noisy and with the emotional impact of a juggernaut. But I couldn't stop smiling with pleasure all the time I was watching it.

This “Dreamgirls” proceeds more as a series of self-contained numbers — the feral “Steppin’to the Bad Side” among them — as opposed to the seamlessly choreographed whole that back in the day left the impression that NewYork’s Imperial Theater was primed for takeoff.
Casey Nicholaw's production is slick but shallow.
Despite fabulous performances from Riley, LaFontaine, Reid and Tyrone Huntley as the group's songwriter CC White, Dreamgirls is predictable, banal and overly sentimental.

cn.t: After a 35-year wait, Dreamgirls explodes onto the West End with megawatt energy and spectacular performances. Critics unanimously agree it's worth the wait, praising its dazzling spectacle and powerhouse vocals.
